Q: How do I handle these many-to-many relationships? A:

A person can do multiple sports, and multiple people can do the same sport. A sport can have multiple risks, and multiple sports can have the same risk. A risk can have multiple precautions, and multiple risks can have the same precaution.

You need the following tables in my opinion:

  • People
  • Activities
  • People Activities
  • Risks
  • Activity Risks
  • Precautions
  • Risk Precautions

Q: How do I implement ToString for my custom primitive type that does not need a Formatter without going against Rust's guidelines? A:

There is, currently, no way to implement ToString in a custom way if you are also implementing Display. However, if you are concerned about the performance of this operation, you shouldn’t be using ToString. Every to_string() call cretes a new String heap allocation, which is likely to be a more significant cost than the Formatter, which has no heap allocation.

When you use Display instead, you can write the text directly to any destination, including as part of a larger formatting operation. This is usually a good choice.

In isolation, the likely most efficient interface your type could possibly offer is a method that returns &'static str, which neither ToString nor Display can be made to do.

(But as with any performance question, the only way to truly know what is best is to try several options and measure the results, preferably using a benchmarking tool.)

Q: Are there recommended lengths for these fields in the user table? A:

For hashed field depend of hashin algoritm for SHA-1 (One used by mysql) value is always 160 bit long, Depending of type of dat you use CHAR or BINARY then for type with 4 bit per character athey need 160/4 = 40 characters. But for 8 bit per character, you need a 160/8 = 20 character long field. If you use the VARCHAR this require an additional byte for the length of the fixed-length field. then

MD5 generates a 128-bit hash value. You can use CHAR(32) or BINARY(16) or VARCHAR(33)

SHA-1 generates a 160-bit hash value. You can use CHAR(40) or BINARY(20) or VARCHAR(41)

SHA-224 generates a 224-bit hash value. You can use CHAR(56) or BINARY(28) or VARCHAR(57)

SHA-256 generates a 256-bit hash value. You can use CHAR(64) or BINARY(32) or or VARCHAR(65)

But normally is used SHA-1

Q: XML sitemap issue A:

This issue is quite common with Rank Math and usually happens due to cache, rewrite rules, or server-level conflicts. Please try the steps below one by one:

  1. Flush Permalinks Again
    Go to WordPress Dashboard → Settings → Permalinks
    Click Save Changes (do not change anything).
    This refreshes rewrite rules.

  2. Check Rank Math Sitemap Settings
    Go to Rank Math → Sitemap Settings

    • Make sure Sitemaps is enabled

    • Ensure Sitemap Index is ON
      Save changes once.

  3. Clear All Caches

    • Clear WordPress cache (plugin cache)

    • Clear hosting/server cache

    • If using Cloudflare or CDN, purge it as well

  4. Check .htaccess File
    Temporarily rename .htaccess to .htaccess_old, then:

    • Go to Settings → Permalinks

    • Click Save Changes to regenerate the file

  5. Disable Other SEO or Sitemap Plugins
    Make sure no other SEO plugin (Yoast, All in One SEO, etc.) or sitemap plugin is active, as this can cause conflicts.

  6. Check Hosting Restrictions
    Some hosting providers block XML files via security/firewall rules.
    Ask your hosting support if /sitemap_index.xml is being blocked.

  7. Test Alternate Sitemap URL
    Try:

    • /sitemap.xml

    • /sitemap_index.xml?rankmath

Q: How can I get the current time in milliseconds in PHP? A:

This works even if you are on 32-bit PHP:

[$usec, $sec] = explode(' ', microtime());

$time_milli = $sec.substr($usec, 2, 3); // '1491536422147'
$time_micro = $sec.substr($usec, 2, 6); // '1491536422147300'

Note this doesn't give you integers, but strings. However this works fine in many cases, for example when building URLs for REST requests.


If you need integers, 64-bit PHP is mandatory.

Then you can reuse the above code and cast to (int):

[$usec, $sec] = explode(' ', microtime());

// these parentheses are mandatory otherwise the precedence is wrong!
//                  ↓                        ↓
$time_milli = (int) ($sec.substr($usec, 2, 3)); // 1491536422147
$time_micro = (int) ($sec.substr($usec, 2, 6)); // 1491536422147300

Or you can use the good ol' one-liners:

$time_milli = (int) round(microtime(true) * 1000);    // 1491536422147
$time_micro = (int) round(microtime(true) * 1000000); // 1491536422147300

Q: How to resolve "ValueError: cannot reindex on an axis with duplicate labels" error while processing time series data in pandas? A:

I think the problem stems from setting a duplicated index first, then doing groupby. Instead, I suggest you group by cube first, then do the interpolation inside each group:

def interp_group(g):
     g.set_index('timestamp', inplace=True)
     g['temp'] = g.temp.interpolate(method="time",limit_direction = "both")
     return g
